text: Structuring is the practice of breaking a large cash transaction into multiple smaller deposits, each below the $10,000 currency transaction report threshold, in order to evade the reporting requirements of 31 U.S.C. 5313(a). It is prohibited under 31 U.S.C. 5324, regardless of whether the underlying funds are derived from a lawful source.

A Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) must be filed by a financial institution within 30 calendar days of detecting facts that may constitute a basis for filing. The narrative should describe who, what, when, where, and why the activity is suspicious, using objective and qualified language rather than conclusory accusations.

Layering is the second stage of money laundering, in which illicit funds are moved through a series of transactions to obscure their origin. Typical indicators include rapid pass-through of funds, transfers through multiple jurisdictions, and the use of accounts with no apparent commercial purpose.

Smurfing refers to the use of multiple individuals, often called money mules, to conduct many small cash deposits across different accounts or branches so that no single transaction triggers a currency transaction report. It is a coordinated form of structuring.

Trade-based money laundering exploits the complexity of international trade to disguise the movement of value. Common techniques include over-invoicing and under-invoicing of goods, multiple invoicing of the same shipment, and misrepresentation of the quality or quantity of traded commodities, as described in FATF guidance.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control administers and enforces economic sanctions programs. U.S. persons must block property and reject transactions involving entities on the Specially Designated Nationals list. A name match alone, without corroborating identifiers such as date of birth or address, may be a false positive subject to disposition by the investigator.

Customer Due Diligence requires financial institutions to identify and verify the identity of customers, understand the nature and purpose of customer relationships to develop a risk profile, and conduct ongoing monitoring to identify and report suspicious transactions.

A currency transaction report must be filed for any transaction in currency of more than $10,000 conducted by, through, or to the financial institution. Multiple currency transactions are treated as a single transaction if the institution has knowledge that they are conducted by or on behalf of the same person and total more than $10,000 in a business day.

Elder financial exploitation indicators include a sudden increase in wire transfers or withdrawals inconsistent with the customer's historical pattern, the addition of new and previously unknown payees, and transactions that appear to be directed by a third party. FinCEN Advisory FIN-2022-A002 describes behavioral red flags.

Shell companies are legal entities that have no significant assets or ongoing business activities. They can be misused to obscure beneficial ownership and to move illicit funds through accounts that lack a legitimate commercial rationale, particularly when incorporated in secrecy jurisdictions.

A risk-based approach to anti-money laundering means allocating compliance resources in proportion to assessed risk. Higher-risk customers, products, and geographies warrant enhanced due diligence, while lower-risk relationships may be subject to simplified measures consistent with regulatory expectations.

Beneficial ownership refers to the natural persons who ultimately own or control a legal entity. Financial institutions must identify beneficial owners at the time a new account is opened for a legal entity customer, generally any individual owning 25 percent or more of the entity and one individual with significant managerial control.

Peeling chains are a layering technique in which a portion of funds is peeled off at each hop in a sequence of transfers, leaving a trail that is difficult to follow. The pattern is characterized by rapid movement and minimal residual balances in intermediary accounts.

Politically exposed persons are individuals who are or have been entrusted with prominent public functions. Relationships with PEPs may present higher money laundering risk due to the potential for corruption, and institutions typically apply enhanced scrutiny to source-of-wealth and source-of-funds information.

Transaction monitoring systems generate alerts based on rules and models that flag activity inconsistent with a customer's expected profile. An alert is not itself evidence of wrongdoing; it is a trigger for investigation, and many alerts are resolved as false positives after analyst review.

The Bank Secrecy Act establishes recordkeeping and reporting requirements for financial institutions to assist government agencies in detecting and preventing money laundering. It requires the filing of currency transaction reports and suspicious activity reports, among other obligations.

Funnel accounts are used to receive cash deposits in one geographic area and withdraw the funds in another, often to move proceeds of crime while avoiding the scrutiny applied to large wire transfers. Frequent same-day deposits and withdrawals in different locations are a red flag.

Source of funds describes the origin of the particular funds used in a transaction, while source of wealth describes the origin of a customer's total assets. Verifying both is central to enhanced due diligence for higher-risk relationships.

Correspondent banking allows a domestic bank to provide services to a foreign respondent bank. Because the domestic institution may have limited visibility into the respondent's underlying customers, correspondent relationships can carry elevated money laundering risk that must be managed through due diligence.

A disposition rationale documents why an alert was not escalated to a SAR. It names the surface red flag that triggered the alert, cites the evidence that resolves it such as the customer's declared business purpose or expected volume, and records the analyst's conclusion that no filing is warranted.

Money laundering generally proceeds in three stages: placement, in which illicit cash enters the financial system; layering, in which the funds are moved to obscure their origin; and integration, in which the laundered funds are returned to the criminal in an apparently legitimate form.

Cash-intensive businesses such as restaurants, car washes, and convenience stores legitimately receive large volumes of cash. This characteristic can also be exploited to commingle illicit proceeds with legitimate receipts, so monitoring focuses on whether deposits are consistent with the declared business profile.

An effective AML program has four pillars: a system of internal controls, independent testing, a designated compliance officer, and ongoing training. A fifth pillar added by the Customer Due Diligence rule requires risk-based procedures for conducting ongoing customer due diligence, including beneficial ownership identification.

Sanctions screening compares customer and counterparty names against watchlists using fuzzy matching to account for spelling variations and transliterations. The strength of a match depends on corroborating identifiers; common names produce frequent false positives that analysts must disposition with documented reasoning.
